Here is a different kind of challenge. Solving it would, I believe, be of some use to the mathlib community.

There is a universe oddity in core Lean which is really hard to pin down. To give an explicit example of this, fire up current mathlib, go to the file Mathlib/RingTheory/Kaehler/Polynomial.lean and look at the first declaration def KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv in that file.

Here's a funny thing about that definition. A few lines above it we have variable (R : Type u). If you change it to variable (R : Type v) (i.e. just rename the universe) then a certain part of Lean runs 30 times quicker when compiling that definition, and nobody really understands why (as far as I know). One step towards analysing this would be to be able to reproduce this phenomenon in core Lean itself without having to import a huge amount of mathlib's commutative algebra. That's the challenge.

Here are more details about the slowdown. The definition is a certain type of isomorphism, and consists of definitions of maps from X to Y and from Y to X, and proofs that composing the maps in both directions gives the identity map. Those proofs are internally called KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv._proof_1 and KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv._proof_2. The thing which becomes 20-30x quicker if you change Type u to Type v is kernel typechecking of these proofs. You can observe this speed-up in the following way. First fire up mathlib and open Mathlib/RingTheory/Kaehler/Polynomial.lean.

1) append

set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true in
set_option trace.profiler true in

just before the docstring of KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv and wait for the
declaration to compile.

2) Click on KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv (which should now be underlined in blue)

3) In the infoview, unfold "All messages" (click on the ▶) and scroll down to the very bottom. Find

[Elab.async] [5578796.000000] ✅️ _private.Lean.AddDecl.0.Lean.addDeclCore ▶

[Elab.async] [5601813.000000] ✅️ _private.Lean.AddDecl.0.Lean.addDeclCore ▶

and click on those ▶s too. You will see something like

[Kernel] [5601746.000000] ✅️ typechecking declarations [KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv._proof_1]

[Kernel] [5578745.000000] ✅️ typechecking declarations [KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv._proof_2]

(the reason I put useHeartbeats true is that the output is then largely machine-independent; if instead we displayed the time in seconds then the results would be highly machine-dependent).

Now change (R : Type u) to (R : Type v) and wham:

[Kernel] [274076.000000] ✅️ typechecking declarations [KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv._proof_1]

[Kernel] [184858.000000] ✅️ typechecking declarations [KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv._proof_2]

(note that those are 6-digit numbers, not 7-digit numbers). In particular, proof_2 is 30x quicker. This has something to do with the fact that the universe of σ is Type u_1, and u_1 is after u but before v in the alphabet. I don't really want to discuss the ins and outs of Lean's universe normalisation algorithm here, this has already been discussed several times before on this chat e.g. #lean4 > kernel universe normalization issue . What I want to emphasize here is that for a long time I have wanted to get to the bottom of this, and and I can't. Let me finish by explaining why I can't.

The core people are adamant that to analyse the issue more closely, they need a reproducer which doesn't import any of mathlib. I have tried manually to rebuild huge chunks of the algebra hierarchy manually but it's hopeless. Kim made mathlib-minimiser https://github.com/kim-em/mathlib-minimizer but I ran it for 2 months on this problem and it still didn't finish. I am wondering whether a modern language model could have a go.

The aim of the challenge is to get a file (which might end up being tens of thousands of lines long) which imports nothing beyond core Lean and ends up with def KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialEquiv with the same proof, and, crucially, where switching R from Type u to Type v causes kernel typechecking to speed up by an order of magnitude. Note that unfortunately this might mean that the proofs need to be sorry-free, which I believe will make this a rather hard challenge, although given what I have seen LLMs doing recently I still have some hope. I am then hoping that the core people will be able to use their tools to analyse what the heck is going on here.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The aim of the challenge is to get a file (which might end up being tens of thousands of lines long)

A naive solution would be to concatenate every module that Kaehler/Polynomial.lean needs, which results in ~450k lines.
Where would you set the bar for a proper solution of this challenge? 10k?
(plus requiring a line-length limit of 100 chars)

Also, would an explanation of the phenomenon (potentially with a lean PR that solves it) be considered a solution, or is the challenge strictly to minimize the example? (though maybe understanding the issue means one could create a small example anyway)

(I'm asking just to clarify the rules as a bystander)

This is not at all the Kahler example, but I believe it is the same phenomenon:

/-
A core-Lean reproducer for a universe-level kernel typechecking cliff.

To test the variant analogous to the Kähler differentials slowdown, run

  lean UniverseOddityCore.lean

and look at the profiler line for `universeOddity`.  Then change the line

  variable (R : Type u)

to

  variable (R : Type v)

and run the same command again.  The generated declaration is definitionally
identical up to the order of universe maxima: with `R : Type u`, the generated
proof compares a binary tree at levels `max u u_1` and `max u_1 u`; with
`R : Type v`, `max u_1 v` is already normalized, so the comparison is
syntactic.
-/

import Lean

open Lean Elab Command

/-- A universe-polymorphic type used by the generated declaration. -/
axiom A.{w} : Type w

/-- A base point of `A`. -/
axiom a.{w} : A.{w}

/-- A binary constructor.  The repeated argument is what makes the mixed-universe
comparison expensive for the kernel. -/
axiom g.{w₀, w₁} : A.{w₀} → A.{w₁} → A.{w₀}

namespace UniverseOddity

/-- The universe used for the `σ` binder in the generated theorem. -/
def sigmaLevel : Level := .param `u_1

/-- `A` at a specified universe level. -/
def mkA (l : Level) : Expr := .const `A [l]

/-- `a` at a specified universe level. -/
def mka (l : Level) : Expr := .const `a [l]

/-- One binary-tree node at a specified universe level. -/
def mkg (l : Level) (x : Expr) : Expr :=
  mkApp2 (.const `g [l, l]) x x

/-- A shared binary tree of depth `n` at universe level `l`. -/
partial def chain (n : Nat) (l : Level) : Expr :=
  match n with
  | 0 => mka l
  | n + 1 => mkg l (chain n l)

/-- The equality type used by the generated theorem. -/
def eqType (lhs rhs : Expr) (l : Level) : Expr :=
  mkApp3 (.const ``Eq [.succ l]) (mkA l) lhs rhs

/-- The reflexivity proof used by the generated theorem. -/
def refl (x : Expr) (l : Level) : Expr :=
  mkApp2 (.const ``Eq.refl [.succ l]) (mkA l) x

/-- Add binders `(R : Type rLevel) (σ : Type u_1)` to a proposition. -/
def withBinders (rLevel : Level) (body : Expr) : Expr :=
  .forallE `R (.sort (.succ rLevel))
    (.forallE `σ (.sort (.succ sigmaLevel)) body .default)
    .default

/-- Add lambdas `(R : Type rLevel) (σ : Type u_1)` to a proof. -/
def withLambdas (rLevel : Level) (body : Expr) : Expr :=
  .lam `R (.sort (.succ rLevel))
    (.lam `σ (.sort (.succ sigmaLevel)) body .default)
    .default

/-- Extract the universe `r` from an elaborated term of type `Type r`. -/
def typeUniverseOf (stx : Syntax) : CommandElabM Level := do
  let ty ← runTermElabM fun _ => do
    let e ← Term.elabTerm stx none
    Meta.whnf (← Meta.inferType e)
  match ty with
  | .sort (.succ rLevel) => pure rLevel
  | _ => throwError "expected a term of type `Type _`, got type{indentExpr ty}"

/--
`add_universe_reproducer R, n` generates a theorem named `universeOddity`.

It uses the raw level `max u_1 r`, where `r` is the universe of `R`, and its
normalized form.  Thus `R : Type u` gives a mixed comparison
`max u u_1` versus `max u_1 u`, while `R : Type v` gives the syntactically
same level `max u_1 v` on both sides.
-/
elab "add_universe_reproducer " r:term ", " n:num : command => do
  let rLevel ← typeUniverseOf r
  let rName ←
    match rLevel with
    | .param n => pure n
    | _ => throwError "expected `R` to live in a universe parameter, got{indentD rLevel}"
  let raw := .max sigmaLevel rLevel
  let normalized := raw.normalize
  let depth := n.getNat
  let lhs := chain depth normalized
  let rhs := chain depth raw
  let type := withBinders rLevel (eqType lhs rhs normalized)
  let value := withLambdas rLevel (refl lhs normalized)
  let levelParams := if rName == `u_1 then [`u_1] else [rName, `u_1]
  liftCoreM <| Lean.addDecl (.thmDecl {
    name := `universeOddity
    levelParams := levelParams
    type := type
    value := value
  })

end UniverseOddity

open UniverseOddity

universe u u_1 v

variable (R : Type u)

set_option trace.profiler.useHeartbeats true in
set_option trace.profiler true in
add_universe_reproducer R, 15

My apologies that the mathlib-minimizer is so slow here.

Have you/anyone tried using the same constraint that mathlib-minimizer uses (i.e. an invariant section at the end, with #guard_msgs blocks that completely determine the behaviour you want to see in the minimization, i.e. both positive and negative behaviours), but just asking an agent to minimize, checking (ideally via a script) after every edit that the invariant section still has no without warnings or errors (and there are no errors before the invariant section of course)?

I've had this work well many times.

Another interesting possibility would be to add an LLM step into mathlib-minimizer, i.e. at some regular interval just tell and LLM to try to minimize, and alternate between mechanical and LLM steps.

But with all of these questions: you need to post exactly the invariant section, using #guard_msgs, that you want, or no one can even get started.
One issue with the minimiser here is that it's hard (perhaps impossible) currently to say "check that this code takes a long time to typecheck".
You could do set_option maxHeartbeats <number> in to set a threshold that is lower than the number the code needs. This should produce a reliable error message.
Yes, it doesn't matter how long it takes to run within reason, as long as there is some deterministic condition. :-)

There is a problem that sometimes the timeout error messages oscillate between mentioning isDefEq and mentioning whnf.

But the substring := true option for #guard_msgs solves this problem.

Sorry to have ignored this thread, I was away for the week.

Snir Broshi said:

A naive solution would be to concatenate every module that Kaehler/Polynomial.lean needs, which results in ~450k lines.
Where would you set the bar for a proper solution of this challenge? 10k?
(plus requiring a line-length limit of 100 chars)

I don't know. I don't understand the rules; it is the FRO asking me to minimise when I come to them whining that something is taking a long time when I import mathlib.

Also, would an explanation of the phenomenon (potentially with a lean PR that solves it) be considered a solution, or is the challenge strictly to minimize the example? (though maybe understanding the issue means one could create a small example anyway)

Really the challenge is not "solve this problem", it is "can AI be used to solve all my minimisation problems".

Here is another example from today. This declaration here https://github.com/plby/Erdos90/blob/8e5bf98e7e69ab3d518289ff5333be19103bc8f5/src/original/Towers/ClassField/HilbertSymbols/Nondegeneracy.lean#L933 , many thousands of lines into an AI-generated project which depends on lots of mathlib, randomly take 4.7 billion mheartbeats to typecheck. The declaration before was fine.

[Elab.async] [4716982214.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▼
  [Kernel] [4716982132.000000] ✅️ typechecking declarations [Towers.CField.HSymbol.hilbert_symbol_artin]

The problem is viral -- every one of the 11 declarations after that until the end of the file also take several minutes to typecheck. Something has gone badly wrong somewhere. But I don't think the FRO can work with this problem. The real challenge is to solve the problem of why this is taking so long. But an intermediate challenge is to figure out how to ask the question in a reasonable way.

This is not at all the Kahler example, but I believe it is the same phenomenon:

But how do we know it's the same phenomenon? Twice before we've come to the FRO saying "we have a universe problem in differential geometry and here is a great minimisation" and twice they have solved the minimised problem and twice it hasn't fixed the main problem. I don't want to waste the FRO's time.

Are there any advanced Lean performance resources one can feed into AI before starting this exploration? Of course, there is the lean checker source code, but what else? Would previous zulip discussions and performance PR be a good idea?

Btw, performance engineering is very common for large software systems once they reach certain scale, so this is all very timely. The way to avoid going back the FRO with problems is to ask the FRO to invest more in canonical performance guides and tools that library maintainers (mathlib or not, human or AI) can use to debug and improve. Some examples from the web world - https://web.dev/learn/performance, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance_API, all the way to arcane tools like https://github.com/mraleph/irhydra or https://v8.dev/blog/system-analyzer. Easier said that done, because latency is cross-cutting, it requires exposing implementation details that are rightfully hidden from general lean usage and change much more often than the currently exposed interfaces.

Michael Stoll said:

You could do set_option maxHeartbeats <number> in to set a threshold that is lower than the number the code needs. This should produce a reliable error message.

I don't think this works for kernel typechecking. I have another minimisation issue and I don't know how to get #guard_msgs to fail iff kernel typechecking is taking too long.
